promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Nov 1 2026, 8 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: Don't make up last week's miles. Heat, short sleep and work stress pushed your easy heart rate up 13 beats, and that is not lost fitness. Next week has about 31 miles, run by heart rate, with a 12-mile long run.

answers.question: I missed Thursday and cut the long run short. Should I make up the miles next week?
answers.answer:
No, let those 9 miles go. Heat, short sleep and a work deadline cost you them. Adding them to next week would pile on more load while you already feel drained.

One short week does not cost you race fitness. What builds it is steady weeks over the next five. Next week is a normal week of about 31 mi, not last week's 36 mi plus the missed 9.

new.analysis:
## Last week against the plan
You ran 27 of the 36 planned miles, and almost none of it was easy. You did Tuesday and Saturday in full, but the heat pushed both into zone 3. You cut Wednesday short, missed Thursday and stopped Sunday 2 miles early.

Stopping Wednesday was the right call. Your reps were slower than the 8:00/mi you held comfortably in early August, and your heart rate was higher. Forcing a third rep would have cost more recovery than it built fitness.

Sunday matters most because the long run is the key session of a marathon build. The heart rate cap was there to keep it aerobic, but your heart rate drifted into zone 4. That made a steady run into a hard one, which is part of why you feel drained now.

## Why it happened
Heat, short sleep and a work deadline all hit at once. Each one raises heart rate at a given pace and slows recovery. Your fitness from early August is still there, but your body carried more load than your running log shows.

Only 10.8 percent of your running time was in zones 1 and 2. With one session a week, most of your time should sit there. Heart rate caps fix this better than pace targets, because pace means little when it is 27 degrees at 6 am.

## Why next week looks like this
Volume stays at a normal level for you, but every easy run has a heart rate cap instead of a pace. The threshold session stays, cut to 1-mile reps, because shorter reps are easier to hold in heat and keep the build moving. The long run is 12 miles, a distance you know, so you can finish it easy rather than just survive it.

The rest days stay as real rest. Sleep is your weak point right now, and an early night does more for Nov 1 than extra miles. The Wednesday swap rule protects you on bad nights without losing the week.

## The road to Nov 1
You are 8 weeks out, and the long run needs to reach about 18 miles, close to 3 hours, by early October. That is still realistic if it grows about 2 miles a week from the week of Sep 7, with a lighter week in late September. Once your sleep is back, Tuesday becomes a medium-long run, and some long runs add miles at marathon pace, about 8:35/mi for 3:45.

settingsProposalBullets: In mid-August you had tightness on the outside of your right knee that settled with hip and glute work and foam rolling, and it is fine now.
In cool weather your easy runs sit around 138 to 140 bpm at about 9:50/mi, and your long runs around 146 bpm.
Your threshold reps run at about 8:00/mi in cool weather.
Hot weather raises your easy heart rate by 10 to 15 bpm, so on hot days you run by heart rate, not pace.

safetyCallouts.title: Know the signs of heat illness.
safetyCallouts.body: If you feel dizzy, confused, sick or chilled, or stop sweating on a run, stop, get into shade and cool down, and get medical help if it does not pass quickly.

safetyCallouts.title: Fatigue that lingers.
safetyCallouts.body: If you still feel tired all the time once your sleep is back to normal, see a doctor before the training load climbs.
